strengths: Extensive empirical validation across many model families (LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, Qwen) and multiple text domains (Wikipedia, news, PubMed), lending broad support to the central correlational claim.

The paper explores several distinct, potentially useful practical applications of the dispersion metric: label-free downstream accuracy estimation, model selection via a 'dispersion gap,' unsupervised layer selection for kNN-LM, and an auxiliary training loss.

Good supporting ablations, including layer-wise analysis, fine-tuning effects (LoRA vs. full FT), and a finer-grained within-cluster vs. between-cluster dispersion analysis that strengthens the main claim beyond trivial explanations.
Clear presentation with abundant figures, appendices, and reported hyperparameters that aid reproducibility of the described experiments.
The topic connects to and extends existing literature on anisotropy/representation degeneration in a way that is potentially actionable rather than purely descriptive.
weaknesses: The core phenomenon (link between anisotropy/dispersion and representation quality) is largely a re-confirmation of well-known findings (e.g., Ethayarajh 2019, Gao et al. 2019) rather than a fundamentally new insight; the contribution is mainly in packaging this as several downstream 'applications.'

The perplexity-vs-dispersion correlations in Figures 3-5 are computed after binning segments by perplexity; binning before correlating can substantially inflate apparent Pearson r by removing within-bin variance, which is a methodological concern not addressed or justified.

The causal training experiment (§4.4) is conducted only on GPT-2-small trained from scratch for just 500-1000 steps, resulting in very high (under-trained) perplexities; the reported 1-4 point single-domain improvements are modest and it is unclear this generalizes to realistic pretraining/fine-tuning regimes at scale.

In §4.2, the 'dispersion gap' is computed on static output-embedding-matrix token vectors rather than the contextual hidden-state representations used to define 'dispersion' everywhere else in the paper, creating an inconsistency in what is actually being measured and claimed as the same phenomenon.

The model-selection experiments in §4.2 use a very small number of checkpoints (9 Qwen variants, 4 Llama/CodeLlama variants), which limits confidence that the strong reported correlations generalize rather than reflect overfitting to a small, curated sample.

No comparison to simple, cheap alternative label-free proxies (e.g., model's own output entropy/confidence, log-likelihood margins) is provided, so it is unclear that dispersion offers a distinct or superior signal for downstream-accuracy prediction or model selection versus these baselines.

Causality between dispersion and predictive quality is not established (and is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation), yet several sections (e.g., 'A Training Signal') implicitly frame dispersion as something to actively optimize for improved performance.

The paper does not engage with the alternative body of work suggesting that reducing anisotropy (e.g., via whitening/isotropy-promoting post-processing) improves representation quality, which appears to be in tension with the paper's 'more dispersion is better' narrative and is not discussed.
Minor: the code repository link in the abstract footnote appears empty/broken, limiting verifiability of reproducibility claims.

strengths: Extensive empirical validation of the perplexity-dispersion relationship across many model families (LLaMA, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral, Phi), multiple domains (Wikipedia, news, medical/scientific text), and at multiple granularities (sequence-level, last-token, varying context lengths).

Rich set of robustness checks in the appendix: generalization to held-out data, an alternative diversity metric (Vendi score) yielding consistent trends, layer-wise and fine-tuning analyses, and a semantic-cluster analysis showing dispersion increases even among highly similar contexts.
The 'squeeze' ablation (explicitly minimizing dispersion) provides some causal evidence beyond pure correlation, showing that suppressing dispersion measurably degrades perplexity.

Four distinct, well-motivated downstream applications (label-free hardness ranking, model selection via a 'dispersion gap', kNN-LM layer selection, and an auxiliary training loss) that go beyond a purely descriptive study and attempt to make the geometric observation actionable.
Large-scale correlation study on Olmo-7B training checkpoints (30 checkpoints) strengthens the model-selection application beyond static cross-model comparisons.
Clear writing, well-organized experiments, and a comprehensive appendix with full numeric tables supporting the main claims.
weaknesses: The core phenomenon (anisotropy/representation collapse relating to model quality) is already well established in prior literature (Ethayarajh 2019; Gao et al. 2019; Li et al. 2020); the paper's main contribution is largely an empirical/practical repackaging rather than a fundamentally new theoretical insight, and the paper offers relatively little rigorous mechanistic explanation for *why* dispersion should predict perplexity beyond intuitive narrative.

Most core claims are correlational; while the squeeze ablation offers some causal signal, it is a single, somewhat crude intervention, and stronger causal or theoretical analysis (e.g., relating dispersion directly to the softmax output entropy via the unembedding matrix) is largely absent.

The label-free hardness-ranking application (§3.1) is explicitly acknowledged to only support ranking within a fixed model/dataset rather than calibrated absolute accuracy estimation, limiting its practical value without an additional calibration step (which itself requires labeled data, partially undermining the 'label-free' framing).

The model-selection 'dispersion gap' metric (§3.2) requires manually curating domain-specific token sets (digits, code keywords, legal terms), which is a nontrivial, task-specific design choice that weakens the claim of a fully generic, label-free tool.

The auxiliary 'push-away' training loss yields only modest improvements in the single-domain setting (1–4 perplexity points), and the more dramatic cross-domain gains could be an somewhat expected/trivial consequence of explicitly separating two very distinct domains (Wiki vs. code) rather than a deep insight about representation geometry.

No code URL is provided (the footnote is left empty), and several other proxy baselines (e.g., alternative unsupervised difficulty/quality signals beyond perplexity) are only partially explored, limiting the strength of comparative claims.
The illustrative Figure 2 appears to be a schematic rather than tied to a specific reported experiment, which could be confusing regarding what is empirically demonstrated versus illustrative.

Evaluation is restricted mostly to English text and standard benchmarks/domains; multilingual results are included in the appendix but multimodal or substantially different domains are not explored, and the generalizability of the relationship to other settings (e.g., non-Transformer architectures) remains untested.

strengths: Extremely broad empirical sweep: many model families (LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, Qwen), many domains (Wikitext, CNN/DailyMail, PubMed), and many context lengths consistently show a negative correlation between dispersion and perplexity, lending some robustness to the core observation.
The paper proposes a simple, cheap, label-free statistic (average pairwise cosine distance) that is easy to compute and could be practically useful as a coarse diagnostic.
Extensive appendix with sanity checks (held-out generalization, Vendi-score cross-validation of the metric, squeeze ablation) shows some effort toward rigor.

The range of proposed use-cases (hardness ranking, model/checkpoint screening, layer selection, training regularizer) demonstrates an attempt at practical relevance beyond a purely descriptive finding.
weaknesses: The central relationship (dispersion vs. perplexity) risks being close to tautological: since next-token probabilities are literally softmax(W_o h), a hidden state that yields a more confident (lower-entropy) prediction will almost mechanically look 'more distinctive' relative to other hidden states under a norm/cosine measure. The paper never disentangles this from a trivial restatement of confidence/logit-norm effects, nor compares against simple baselines like softmax entropy or max-prob as competing 'geometric-free' hardness signals.

The paper conflates several very different notions under the single term 'dispersion': final-token embedding spread across unrelated segments (§2), spread within a semantic cluster (§2.3), sub-layer output spread for kNN-LM key selection (§3.3), and static output-embedding-matrix distances for specific token subsets (§3.2). These are conceptually distinct constructs bundled together for narrative coherence, which weakens the precision and generality of the central claim.

Section 3.3 (layer selection for kNN-LM) never actually runs the full kNN-LM pipeline or reports interpolated perplexity; it only shows that attention outputs have higher dispersion than FFN outputs and cites a prior paper (Xu et al., 2023) for the actual kNN-LM result. The claimed practical application is therefore unvalidated end-to-end.

The model-selection application (§3.2) relies on hand-picked, domain-specific token subsets (digits for math, keywords for code) engineered per task; this is not clearly a generalizable methodology and could simply reflect the fact that fine-tuned models spread out familiar/task-relevant vocabulary in the embedding matrix — an already well-known effect of domain adaptation, not a novel geometric insight.

The training-time application (§3.4) yields quite modest single-domain gains (1–4 perplexity points on values in the 80–230 range) that could easily fall within noise/hyperparameter variance; the more impressive cross-domain gains stem from explicitly pushing apart embeddings from different domains, which is a different (and more trivial) mechanism than the paper's headline claim about within-domain dispersion driving lower perplexity, yet it is presented as support for the same unified narrative.

The paper's contribution relative to substantial prior work on anisotropy/representation degeneration/intrinsic dimension (Ethayarajh 2019; Gao et al. 2019; Li et al. 2020; Valeriani et al. 2023, etc.) is largely incremental — introducing one more scalar summary statistic and running it across many settings, rather than new theoretical understanding of why or when dispersion is causally linked to quality.

Causality is asserted rhetorically ('functional driver,' 'causal link') based only on the squeeze ablation, which conflates suppressing dispersion with directly perturbing the loss landscape in a way that could hurt optimization for many unrelated reasons, not specifically because of dispersion per se.

The perplexity-vs-dispersion binning procedure (uniform sampling of bins, chosen to cover 'both tails') introduces potential selection artifacts, and the comparison in Appendix B.1.2 claiming perplexity 'fails' as a hardness signal seems suspicious/under-explained, since perplexity should trivially correlate with correctness at the individual level; the aggregated binning procedure design may be responsible for washing out that signal rather than a real limitation of perplexity.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical validation of the central perplexity–dispersion correlation across many model families (LLaMA, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral, Phi), scales, and domains (WikiText, CNN/DailyMail, PubMed), with consistently significant Pearson correlations reported in both the main text and an extensive appendix.

The paper goes beyond a single observation to propose and test four distinct, practically useful applications (label-free hardness ranking, model/checkpoint selection via a 'dispersion gap', layer selection for kNN-LM, and an auxiliary training loss), which strengthens the case that the geometric quantity is actionable rather than merely descriptive.

Good robustness checks: replication with an alternative diversity metric (Vendi Score), a held-out/test-split generalization check, a distribution-shift study across HellaSwag/IFEval/QuAIL, and a calibration analysis mapping dispersion to estimated accuracy with small MAE.

The 'squeeze' ablation (explicitly minimizing dispersion) provides some evidence toward a causal (not merely correlational) relationship between representation geometry and predictive performance, which is a nice complement to the purely correlational main results.

Clear and well-organized related-work discussion that appropriately differentiates the contribution from the closely related but purely descriptive prior work (Viswanathan et al., 2025) and from mechanistic-interpretability/probing lines of work.
Reproducibility details (hyperparameters, datasets, model checkpoints) are given in substantial appendix detail.
weaknesses: The central finding — that confidently predicted contexts occupy more distinct regions of embedding space while uncertain contexts cluster near the mean — is a fairly intuitive consequence of how softmax-based next-token prediction interacts with anisotropic embedding spaces (well documented since Ethayarajh 2019/Gao et al. 2019); the paper does not clearly rule out this more mundane explanation or otherwise establish that dispersion carries information beyond a proxy for prediction confidence/peakiness.

The kNN-LM application (§3.3) is only indirectly validated: the paper measures layer-wise dispersion and cites Xu et al. (2023) for the claim that attention-layer keys improve kNN-LM performance, but never actually runs the full kNN-LM retrieval pipeline to confirm that the dispersion-selected layer indeed yields the best perplexity, weakening the claimed practical shortcut.

The 'push-away' training results (§3.4) are modest in the single-domain setting (roughly 1–4 perplexity points out of ~100–200 baseline perplexity, i.e., a few percent), and the more impressive cross-domain gains could partly reflect the auxiliary loss implicitly encoding domain identity into the hidden state (an easier, somewhat trivial signal) rather than a deeper geometric improvement in language modeling quality.

Several core validation experiments (e.g., Figure 8, §3.1) use synthetic slices constructed by mixing known correct/incorrect examples at target proportions, which is somewhat circular for testing an unlabeled 'hardness ranking' use case; the more realistic calibration experiment in the appendix still requires a labeled calibration subset, so the fully label-free framing is only partially substantiated.

Correlational evidence for the model-selection application partly relies on very small numbers of checkpoints per family (e.g., ~9 Qwen models), which limits the reliability of the reported Spearman correlations (>0.95) despite the supporting Olmo-7B trajectory analysis (N=30) being more convincing.

Novelty is incremental relative to a substantial existing literature on anisotropy, embedding geometry, and contrastive/repulsive training losses (explicitly acknowledged in the Related Work and Appendix B.4.3); the paper's contribution is largely in breadth of empirical demonstration and practical packaging rather than a fundamentally new mechanism or theory.

The appendix is very large relative to the main paper, and some key claims (e.g., causality, generalizability of the dispersion gap beyond in-family comparisons) remain only partially addressed, as acknowledged in the Limitations section.
